          "text": "# Ptolemy\u2019s Cluster: A Southern-Sky Gathering\n\n*An ancient-looking patch of stars gets a modern measure: NGC 6475\u2019s coordinates, motion and distance point observers toward a rich field in Scorpius.*\n\nThere is a particular pleasure in finding a star cluster before reaching for a telescope: first a small brightening among the stars, then a gathering that resolves into points. Ptolemy\u2019s Cluster\u2014catalogued as NGC 6475\u2014is an open cluster, a group of stars associated in space rather than a distant galaxy or a cloud of glowing gas. The SIMBAD astronomical database identifies NGC 6475 as an open cluster and gives its position in the southern sky: right ascension 17h 53m 47.3s, declination \u221234\u00b0 50\u2032 28\u2033. [SIMBAD: NGC 6475](https://simbad.cds.unistra.fr/simbad/sim-id?Ident=NGC%206475)\n\nThose coordinates make the cluster\u2019s visibility strongly dependent on where you observe from. At latitude 35\u00b0 south, it passes almost overhead. At 40\u00b0 north, it reaches only about 15\u00b0 above the southern horizon at its highest point, where haze and buildings can easily interfere. The declination is the key: a negative value places the target south of the celestial equator. Choose a site with a clear southern horizon, and observe when the cluster is high for your location.\n\nSIMBAD lists a parallax of 3.5704 milliarcseconds. A simple inversion of that value puts the cluster roughly 280 parsecs away\u2014about 910 light-years. This is an estimate from the parallax, not a claim that every star in the field has been individually weighed or placed at precisely the same distance.
